power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 571 columns across 80 data files.
#### Issues Identified

2 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 80 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}

), Basis = c("none", "dependency")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: `code/CKM_US_Main_public.R` to `CKM_US_Main_public.R` (in CKM_US_Main_public.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file. **49 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Missing inputs
2 input files the code reads are in the deposit but not usable as named: too large to download, inside an archive, or under a similar name.
#### Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 11 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `06_spmoran_resf.rds`, `06_inla_bym2.rds`, `02_ckm_index.rds`, `01_tracts_geo.rds`, `12_bym2_refit_model1.rds`, `06_6g_inla_bym2_nobehav.rds`, `12_bym2_refit_model2.rds`, `07_shap.rds`, `04_nhanes_individual.rds`, `06_5d_residual_variogram.rds`, `01_places_tract.rds`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 0 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 1 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. text.text: Background.
The American Heart Association defined Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome in 2023.
Census-tract studies often examined one condition without spatial modeling.
It is unclear where combined Stage 1-2 burden concentrates and how it relates to aging, environment, and socioeconomic conditions.
Methods.

We built a CKM burden index for 70,336 tracts from five CDC PLACES crude prevalences (obesity, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, chronic kidney disease) and compared it with NHANES 2017-2020.

In 69,530 contiguous-U.S. tracts, we fit Bayesian spatial (BYM2) models with demographic, socioeconomic, and environmental predictors and aging × environment interactions, plus descriptive machine learning.
The primary model excluded behavioral measures sharing the outcome's BRFSS source; a second added them.
Credible intervals (CrIs) are conditional on PLACES estimates.
Results.
Agreement with NHANES was modest.
Burden clustered spatially (Moran's I = 0.657) and highest in the South.
Behavioral measures had the largest machine-learning importance (52.6%), partly from shared sourcing.
Each percentage-point increase in adults ≥65 years was associated with 0.112 units higher burden (95% CrI 0.111-0.113) outside low-income, lowaccess (LILA) tracts.
LILA tracts had 0.10-0.14 units higher burden from the 25th aging percentile but not consistently in the youngest decile.
Aging and socioeconomic associations held across sensitivity analyses.
The primary model's residual Southern excess approached zero after adding behavioral measures, which may reflect shared measurement, real differences in these behaviors, or both.
Conclusions.
CKM burden is spatially clustered and highest in the South.
LILA tracts had modestly higher burden above the youngest tracts.
These cross-sectional estimates support area-level surveillance and needs assessment.

Besag-York-Mollié 2 spatial model CKM cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic CrI credible interval ESF eigenvector spatial filtering HOLC Home Owners' Loan Corporation ICE Index of Concentration at the Extremes INLA integrated nested Laplace approximation LILA low-income, low-access tract flag (USDA Food Access Research Atlas) LISA local indicators of spatial association NHANES National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey OLS ordinary least squares PC1 first principal component PLACES Population Level Analysis and Community Estimates (CDC) RUCA Rural-Urban Commuting Area SDOH social determinants of health SHAP Shapley additive explanations Wx spatially lagged (neighborhood) predictor values XGBoost extreme gradient boosting
What Is New?
• Across 69,530 US census tracts, a combined cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic burden index built from CDC PLACES was clustered in space and highest across the South.
• Each 1-percentage-point higher share of adults aged ≥65 years was associated with 0.112 units higher burden (crude prevalence, not age-standardized).
What Are the Clinical Implications?

In October 2023, the American Heart Association issued a presidential advisory that recast the conditions of obesity, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, hypertension, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease into a single integrated term: Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome 1 .
text.formatted: In October 2023, the American Heart Association issued a presidential advisory that recast the conditions of obesity, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, hypertension, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease into a single integrated term: Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> .

text.text: The advisory introduced a four-stage framework, from Stage 0 (no risk factors) through Stage 1 (excess or dysfunctional adiposity), Stage 2 (metabolic risk factors and/or moderate-to-high-risk CKD), Stage 3 (subclinical cardiovascular disease or very-high-risk CKD), and Stage 4 (clinical cardiovascular disease, including kidney failure subcategory 4b), and called for action on the social determinants of health that pattern progression through these stages.

Because the intensity of monitoring and treatment escalates across these stages, identifying which populations and places carry the greatest CKM burden is central to directing screening, prevention, and management.
Population aging, structural disadvantage, and environmental exposure might shape the geography of CKM burden.
For instance, adults aged ≥65 years make up about 16.8% of the U.S. population, and the prevalence of every CKM component rises steeply with age 2, 3 .
text.formatted: For instance, adults aged ≥65 years make up about 16.8% of the U.S. population, and the prevalence of every CKM component rises steeply with age <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: The unequal geography of structural disadvantage is captured by Krieger's Index of Concentration at the Extremes (ICE) 4 , whose association with cardiometabolic outcomes persists after individuallevel adjustment 5, 6 .
text.formatted: The unequal geography of structural disadvantage is captured by Krieger's Index of Concentration at the Extremes (ICE) <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> , whose association with cardiometabolic outcomes persists after individuallevel adjustment <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: Long-term ambient air pollution is associated with cardiopulmonary mortality 7 , summarized in an AHA scientific statement 8 , and with chronic kidney disease and diabetes 9, 10 ; prospective evidence links pollutant mixtures to the onset and progression of cardio-renal-metabolic multimorbidity itself 11 .
text.formatted: Long-term ambient air pollution is associated with cardiopulmonary mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> , summarized in an AHA scientific statement <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> , and with chronic kidney disease and diabetes <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> ; prospective evidence links pollutant mixtures to the onset and progression of cardio-renal-metabolic multimorbidity itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: The nearest prior nationwide tract-level analysis compared seven composite neighborhood indices against median household income as predictors of coronary heart disease, stroke, and chronic kidney disease, with obesity, hypertension, and diabetes as secondary outcomes, and found similar associations 12 .
text.formatted: The nearest prior nationwide tract-level analysis compared seven composite neighborhood indices against median household income as predictors of coronary heart disease, stroke, and chronic kidney disease, with obesity, hypertension, and diabetes as secondary outcomes, and found similar associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Two of those outcomes, coronary heart disease and stroke, are Stage 4 clinical endpoints in the AHA framework.
However, where the combined Stage 1-2 CKM burden that precedes them concentrates, once spatial dependence is modeled, has not been described nationally at the census-tract level.
It is also unknown whether this burden is highest in tracts whose populations are older and more exposed to environmental hazards.

We construct a continuous tract-level index of the AHA CKM Stage 1-2 burden using CDC PLACES estimates of the five core cardiometabolic indicators and compare it against National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2017-2020 individual-level co-occurrence patterns.

Then, we relate the index to demographic, socioeconomic, and environmental predictors in a hierarchical Bayesian BYM2 spatial regression, cross-checked by ordinary least squares with residual-autocorrelation diagnostics, and in an XGBoost/SHAP machine-learning model ( §S2.4).
All formal inferential claims rest on the spatial regression models; the machinelearning model is exploratory and is not used to test population-level hypotheses.
We address four aims: 1.
Construction and external comparison.

Construct a tract-level CKM burden index that summarizes the prevalence of five conditions in the AHA Stage 1-2 framework and characterize its agreement with independent individual-level NHANES estimates.
Correlate decomposition.

Quantify the relative contribution of demographic, socioeconomic, and environmental predictors to the spatial distribution of CKM burden using inference from the spatial regression and exploratory decomposition from the machine-learning model.
Aging × environment interaction.
Examine whether associations between neighborhood environmental characteristics and CKM burden differ according to the proportion of residents aged ≥65 years.
Behavioral-block contrast.

Quantify how much of the socioeconomic-concentration signal is carried by the co-reported behavioral and healthcare-engagement block, by comparing an otherwise identical pair of spatial models fit with and without that block.

This is a cross-sectional, ecological analysis of U.S. census tracts using publicly available, deidentified secondary data; it did not constitute human-subjects research requiring institutional review board approval.
Dr Batobara had full access to all the data in the study and takes responsibility for its integrity and the data analysis.
Reporting follows the STROBE and RECORD guidelines (Supplemental Methods).

The outcome is a continuous tract-level CKM burden index: the first principal component of five crude, non-age-standardized CDC PLACES 2022 tract prevalences (obesity, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and self-reported chronic kidney disease), oriented so that higher values denote greater burden 13 .
text.formatted: The outcome is a continuous tract-level CKM burden index: the first principal component of five crude, non-age-standardized CDC PLACES 2022 tract prevalences (obesity, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and self-reported chronic kidney disease), oriented so that higher values denote greater burden <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: We used the 2022 release because the 2023 release has no Florida estimates for measures based on 2021 BRFSS data and the 2024 release no longer includes chronic kidney disease.
Agreement with independent individual-level data was assessed against NHANES 2017-2020 14 ( §3.1).
text.formatted: Agreement with independent individual-level data was assessed against NHANES 2017-2020 <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> ( §3.1).

text.text: We grouped the predictors into four blocks.
Table S1a lists the source, year, spatial resolution, and units of each variable.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">S1a</ref> lists the source, year, spatial resolution, and units of each variable.

text.text: The demographic block includes the percentage of adults aged ≥65 years and the percentage of Hispanic or Latino residents.

The socioeconomic block includes Krieger's Index of Concentration at the Extremes for race and for income, the percentage of adults with a bachelor's degree or higher, and rurality from USDA Rural-Urban Commuting Area codes 15 .
text.formatted: The socioeconomic block includes Krieger's Index of Concentration at the Extremes for race and for income, the percentage of adults with a bachelor's degree or higher, and rurality from USDA Rural-Urban Commuting Area codes <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: The environmental block includes air pollution (PM₂.₅ and ozone, from the EPA Downscaler), warm-season heat (mean daily maximum temperature from May to September, from PRISM 16 ), walkability (EPA National Walkability Index 17 ), and food access.
text.formatted: The environmental block includes air pollution (PM₂.₅ and ozone, from the EPA Downscaler), warm-season heat (mean daily maximum temperature from May to September, from PRISM <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> ), walkability (EPA National Walkability Index 17 ), and food access.

text.text: For food access, we used the USDA flag for low-income, low-access (LILA) tracts (1-mile/10-mile definition), because it requires both low income and poor access to food.
The behavioral and healthcareengagement block includes four more PLACES measures: physical inactivity, smoking, routine checkups, and lack of health insurance.
Supplemental Methods explains how we assigned the air pollution and temperature values to each tract.
Our main analysis used a hierarchical Bayesian spatial regression.
Each tract had a random effect with a scaled BYM2 prior, which lets tract effects be spatially structured, unstructured, or a mix of both.
Neighbors were each tract's 8 nearest tracts (k = 8).
We fit the models by integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA) with penalized-complexity priors.
Continuous predictors in interaction terms were mean-centered.
We report each association as a posterior mean with a 95% credible interval (CrI) and call it credible when the interval excludes zero.
When a result combines several coefficients, such as the LILA contrast at a given age composition, we computed it from the joint posterior rather than from the separate intervals.
The CrIs are conditional on the PLACES estimates; that is, they treat those estimates as fixed.
They do not include the uncertainty of the PLACES model itself, whose shared county-and state-level random effects make errors correlated across tracts ( §S3.7).
We fit two models on the same tracts.
Model 1, the primary model, excludes the behavioral and healthcare-engagement block; Model 2 includes it.
The two models answer different questions and comparing them is one of our aims.
Model 1 is primary because the behavioral measures come from the same BRFSS survey cycles as the outcome, so adjusting for them may remove part of the associations we want to study.

Several demographic and socioeconomic predictors are also inputs to the PLACES model ( §4.5), but we keep them because they are the structure under study, whereas the behavioral measures are candidate mediators.
We used ordinary least squares, with checks for residual spatial autocorrelation, and eigenvector spatial filtering as cross-checks.
We also fit a tuned XGBoost model with SHAP values, which we report descriptively only.

To test the shape of the aging association, we refit Model 1 with a natural spline for % age ≥65 years (df = 4, with df = 3 and 5 as sensitivity checks; §S2.4) and compared the fits by log marginal likelihood ( §3.3; Table S13).

Then, we excluded Alaska, Hawaii, and tracts with missing covariates, which left 69,530 tracts (Table 1).

text.text: We used this sample for both the OLS baseline ( §3.2) and the BYM2 regression ( §3.3).
The first principal component (PC1) explained 76.1% of the variance in the five indicators, and all five loadings were positive and similar in size (range 0.36-0.49; Table 2).

text.text: We compared PLACES with individual-level NHANES 2017-2020 data (Table 2, Figure 1; Supplemental Results).

text.text: National prevalences were similar for diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and chronic kidney disease, differing by 0.30 to 2.23 percentage points.
Obesity was 8.95 percentage points lower in PLACES, as expected, because BRFSS relies on selfreported height and weight, whereas NHANES measures them.
The relationships among the indicators agreed less well.
When we compared the ten pairwise correlations in PLACES with those in NHANES, they agreed only weakly (r = 0.37), and the PC1 loadings agreed even less (r = 0.16).

This is consistent with how PLACES estimates are produced: the five indicators are much more correlated in PLACES (mean |r| = 0.69) than in NHANES (mean |r| = 0.16), and all ten pairs are more correlated in PLACES (Supplemental Note 2).

text.text: The tract-level index of AHA Stage 1-2 CKM burden was clustered in space ( §3.2) and agreed only modestly with NHANES individual-level data.

The closest prior study is the nationwide analysis by Krishnan et al. (2026), which compared seven composite neighborhood indices with median household income as predictors of coronary heart disease, stroke, and chronic kidney disease and found similar associations.
Our study differs in four ways.

First, their primary outcomes, coronary heart disease and stroke, are Stage 4 clinical disease, whereas our index measures the earlier Stage 1-2 CKM burden; they analyzed obesity, hypertension, and diabetes only as separate secondary outcomes.
Second, we model a single index aligned with CKM Stages 1-2 and compared with NHANES, rather than comparing social indices with income.
Third, they adjusted for tract median age, whereas we used the share of adults aged ≥65 years, the group in which CKM conditions are most common.
We also test this share as an effect modifier, and because our outcome is not age-standardized, our aging terms reflect both the age makeup of tracts and age-related risk.
Fourth, our BYM2 model accounts for spatial autocorrelation, whereas their non-spatial regressions treat tracts as independent.
When we refit our primary model on an extended index that adds their Stage 4 endpoints, every coefficient kept its sign and the Southern excess remained ( §S3.9).

Our study therefore addresses two questions theirs did not: where Stage 1-2 burden concentrates once spatial dependence is modeled, and whether age composition modifies its environmental associations.
We know of no direct precedent at the U.S. tract scale for the LILA difference, which was present across most of the age distribution but absent in the youngest tracts ( §3.3).

Four limitations matter most for interpretation.
First, the design is ecological.
It compares tracts, not individuals, so our coefficients should not be read as individual-level effects.
Second, the outcome and several predictors are partly circular.
The CDC PLACES model predicts tract prevalence from age, sex, race and ethnicity, education, and county poverty, which overlap with predictors in our models.
Part of the demographic and socioeconomic associations may therefore come from the PLACES model itself, and the index should be read as a proxy for burden, not a measure of clinical CKM co-morbidity.
Our credible intervals also treat the PLACES estimates as fixed, so they do not include the uncertainty of the PLACES model ( §S3.7).
Third, each model is open to a different bias.
Model 1 omits the behavioral block and may be confounded by it.
Model 2 adjusts for the block, which shares a data source with the outcome and may lie on the causal pathway, so it may be over-adjusted.
Fourth, the routine-checkup and health-insurance estimates may reflect ascertainment and reverse causation.
PLACES measures diagnosed conditions, so tracts with better access to care can show higher measured burden at the same level of disease.
The cross-sectional design also cannot rule out people moving because of their health.

Supplemental Note 2 describes these limitations in full, along with sensitivity to spatial scale, exposure measurement error, multiple comparisons, the crude (not age-standardized) outcome, and the exclusion of New Jersey.

Future studies should test whether these patterns hold in later CDC PLACES releases, use difference-in-differences designs to test whether changes in food access precede changes in CKM burden, and use individual-level data, such as NHANES and geocoded cohorts, to separate confounding from mediation (Supplemental Discussion).
At the U.S. census-tract scale, CKM burden is spatially clustered.

In the analysis, the behavioral and healthcare-engagement measures ranked highest, followed by population aging, with smaller contributions from environmental exposures and structural socioeconomic conditions.
This ranking is not causal since the behavioral measures come from the same BRFSS data as the outcome.
LILA tracts had modestly higher burden across most of the age distribution, but evidence that age composition changes environmental associations was limited.

A Southern excess in burden remained after adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, and environmental factors and approached zero only when the shared-source behavioral measures were added, so its causes remain unknown.
These estimates support area-level surveillance and needs assessment.
